title: Dwarf Galaxy WLM (NIRCam Image)
caption: Part of the dwarf galaxy WLM, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: Wolf–Lundmark–Melotte (WLM) · constellation Cetus · about About 3 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Kristen McQuinn (Rutgers University); Image Processing: Zoltan Levay (STScI)

recognition.text: NASA Webb image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Thousands of separate points and smudges fill this frame, stars and background galaxies of many colors, sizes, shapes and brightnesses. Together they make up part of the dwarf galaxy Wolf–Lundmark–Melotte, or WLM, captured by the Near-Infrared Camera on the James Webb Space Telescope.

WLM is a barred, irregular dwarf galaxy about 3 million light-years away in the constellation Cetus. A dwarf galaxy is a small galaxy with far fewer stars than the Milky Way, and an irregular one lacks a tidy spiral or elliptical form.

NASA released this image to show how well Webb can resolve faint stars beyond the Milky Way. Here the galaxy is resolved into individual stars, each a separate point of light. More distant galaxies show through behind them and add to the crowd of objects in the field. The frame shows only a portion of WLM, not the whole galaxy.
scale: NASA lists this view as about 2 arcminutes across, roughly 1,700 light-years at the object’s distance.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam captured this in near-infrared light. NASA shows F090W (0.9 micron) in blue, F150W (1.5 micron) in cyan, F250M (2.5 micron) in yellow and F430M (4.3 micron) in red.
understand.eye: These wavelengths are longer than red light and invisible to the eye.
